podcast.title: Failed Move to New York (1971)
podcast.body: In 1971, Gino Vannelli relocated to New York City to pursue a music career, but this initial attempt was unsuccessful, leading him to return home temporarily. "Now, Gina Vannelly moved to New York in 1971 to try to make a go of a career in music and it did not work."

Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Audience Demographics (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Gino Vannelli estimated that approximately 8% of his audience was black, with the notable exception of Los Angeles where a "sophistication among white rock audiences" resulted in a proportionally larger white demographic for his shows. "He said, probably about 8% of the audience is black except in LA where there's a sophistication among white rock audiences that make them proportionally a larger part."

Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Assessment of Early 70s Canadian Music Scene
podcast.body: Gino Vannelli held the view that Canada was not adequately prepared to produce high-quality records in the early 1970s, specifically citing the years 1970, 1971, and 1972 as periods where the industry lacked the necessary development. "He said that Canada was not ready to make good records in 70s, 71, 72."

srcs.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Belief in 1980s Canadian Production Improvement
podcast.body: Gino Vannelli believed that Canada's capacity to produce "world-class" records did not truly begin until the 1980s, when artists like Celine Dion and Bryan Adams contributed to elevating production standards. "He didn't think that that began to happen until the 1980s. And he cited Celine Dion and Brian Adams as artists that elevated the production of records."

Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Confronting Herb Alpert at A&M Records
podcast.body: In Los Angeles in the mid-70s, Gino Vannelli made a daring "mad dash" past the security gates at A&M Records to directly confront Herb Alpert and plead his case for a chance in the music industry, a move that would be highly improbable today. "made a mad dash past the gates at A&M records toward Herb Alpert. And pleaded his case with Herb Alpert."

srcs.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: First White Singer on Soul Train
podcast.body: Gino Vannelli made history as the first white singer to perform on the iconic television show "Soul Train," which was primarily dedicated to showcasing black artists. "Geno was the first white singer to perform on Soul Train."

Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Relocation to Los Angeles (Mid-70s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, Gino Vannelli made another attempt to establish his music career in the United States, this time relocating to Los Angeles after his earlier failure in New York. "He went back to the United States this time. He was in Los Angeles in the mid 70s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Soul Train Appearance and Identity Surprise
podcast.body: Don Cornelius, the legendary host of "Soul Train," was reportedly surprised upon meeting Gino Vannelli to discover he was not black but a white artist from Montreal, as Vannelli's sound often incorporated elements of soul and R&B. "Imagine his surprise when he met Geno Van Elly and realized he was not black. But he was a white guy from Montreal."

srcs.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s

podcast.title: Soul Train's Impact on African American Fanbase
podcast.body: Gino Vannelli attributed a significant portion of his African American fanbase to his pioneering appearance on "Soul Train." "He said after his appearance on Soul Train, that's kind of what got him a lot of his African American fan base."
